chunks: PCB insulation materials and trade-offs. The question: What materials are often used for the insulation materials? What are their tradeoffs?
The insulating material between a board's copper layers is called the dielectric.
It holds the layers apart, but it also shapes how fast signals travel, how much of a fast signal is lost, how well heat escapes, and whether the board survives soldering.
The standard material, FR-4, is cheap and fine for most boards. Special materials are used when a job needs less signal loss or better heat flow.
Think of the surface of a road. Ordinary asphalt is cheap and works well at city speeds. A race car at top speed needs a much smoother track, and a good one costs far more.
Signals behave the same way. At low frequency FR-4 is fine. At several GHz (billions of cycles per second) it quietly eats away part of the signal, so you pay for a better "road".
The analogy is loose: the loss comes from the material soaking up energy and turning it into heat, not from friction.
At 5 gigahertz, FR-4 loses about 0.
4 decibels per inch in the dielectric alone (a 10 inch trace loses 4 decibels, plus conductor loss), while a ceramic-filled RF laminate loses about 0.
07 decibels/inch and PTFE about 0. 015. Because the curves are straight lines on log-log axes, the ratio between materials is constant.
The mid-loss curve is representative of "low-loss" epoxy-glass grades: exact values are product-specific.
Dielectric constant ( r ): how strongly the material stores electric field. It sets trace widths and signal speed ("Dielectrics and permittivity").
Loss tangent ( delta ): how much signal energy the material absorbs. Smaller is better ("Dielectric losses and their mechanisms").
Glass transition ( T g ): the temperature where the resin turns soft and expands quickly. Decibel (dB): a ratio scale for loss.
3 decibels is half the power, 10 decibels is a tenth. FR-4: glass cloth in epoxy, the standard board material ("What "FR4" means").
Send a 5 gigahertz signal along a 10 inch trace. On FR-4 the dielectric alone loses about 0. 41 decibels per inch, so 10 inches lose about 4 decibels.
That leaves about 40% of the power. On a ceramic-filled RF (radio-frequency) laminate with 0. 07 decibels per inch, the same trace loses about 0. 7 decibels and keeps about 85%.
At 1 gigahertz FR-4 loses only about 0. 08 decibels per inch, which is why it is fine for most products. That is the whole idea.
"The default is FR-4, glass-fibre in epoxy: cheap, strong and easy to process, with a dielectric constant around 4. 3 and a loss tangent around 0.
02, fine up to about a gigahertz. Its limits are high-frequency loss, a permittivity that varies, a modest glass transition and poor heat conduction.
Alternatives: high-Tg FR-4 for lead-free assembly, polyimide for flex and heat, PTFE or ceramic-filled laminates with loss of 0. 001 to 0.
004 for RF, ceramics for heat and high temperature, and metal-core for LEDs. It's a trade between loss, temperature, thermal conduction and cost."
